title: Why Weight Fluctuates Day to Day
summary: Seeing the scale move up after a good day isn't a failure. Daily weight swings of 1–3 kg are normal and rarely reflect actual fat change.

steps.heading: Your weight is not your fat
steps.body: The number on the scale reflects everything in your body at that moment — bones, muscle, organs, blood, water, food in transit, and fat. Of all these, body fat is the slowest to change. A single pound of fat requires a deficit of roughly 3,500 calories. A 1 kg overnight gain almost never means you've stored a kilogram of fat — it means something else has changed.

steps.heading: Water retention is the main driver
steps.body: Your body stores and releases water constantly in response to what you eat and drink. Carbohydrates cause water retention — for every gram of glycogen stored in your muscles, your body holds about 3 grams of water alongside it. A high-carb day can add 1–2 kg of water weight by the next morning. Eating salty food, hormonal shifts, and inflammation all have similar effects.

steps.heading: The digestive pipeline
steps.body: Food doesn't pass through your system instantly. The weight of food and liquid you've consumed but not yet digested or excreted is part of the number you see. Eating a large late dinner, changing your eating schedule, or any factor that slows digestion — including stress or reduced physical activity — can easily account for 0.5–1.5 kg of variation that has nothing to do with fat.

steps.heading: Hormones and the menstrual cycle
steps.body: Estrogen and progesterone fluctuations during the menstrual cycle cause significant water retention, particularly in the luteal phase (the two weeks before menstruation). Increases of 1–3 kg are common and completely normal. These shifts can obscure genuine fat loss progress over short timescales and lead to unnecessary discouragement.

steps.heading: How to use the scale constructively
steps.body: Weigh yourself at the same time each day (morning, after using the toilet, before eating) if you want reliable comparisons. Focus on weekly or monthly trends rather than daily readings. Plotting a 7-day or 14-day rolling average smooths out the noise and reveals the real direction your weight is heading. A single reading means almost nothing in isolation.

takeaway: Daily weight swings are a normal feature of physiology, not a reflection of your effort. What matters is the trend over weeks, not the number on any given morning.
